---
<!-- theorem--1: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 1.1]{arxiv}
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:cloperator}
coker \Big( Haar_{n,n}(\mathbb{Z}_p) \Big) 
\end{equation} is a \textit{reversible} Markov chain on abelian $p$-groups.
<!-- end theorem--1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The process (\ref{eqn:cloperator}) is a direct generalization of the process (\ref{eqn:process}). Indeed, the cokernel is a direct generalization of the corank, as for a matrix $M$ over a finite field $k$, \[ coker(M) \cong k^{corank(M)}. \]
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:maintheorem}
Let $R$ be a finite or profinite local ring. Then $coker(Haar_{n,n+u}(R))$ is a reversible Markov chain, for any $u \in \mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
In fact, we prove more. The random variable $coker(Haar_{n,m}(R))$ is a "two-dimensional" Markov chain, governed by a certain family of transition operators. We refer to \S \ref{sec:randomoperators} for more details.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
By itself, the \textit{Markov property} is not surprising, and can be deduced from the following two facts:
\begin{itemize}
\item Suppose that a module is defined as a set of generators satisfying linear relations. Adding another Haar random relation has the effect of modding out by a Haar random element of this module.
\item The module $\text{coker}(M)$ is uniquely determined by $\text{coker}(M^T)$ and the dimensions of $M$.
\end{itemize}
Indeed, the first fact tells us what happens to the cokernel when we add a Haar random column vector to a matrix. The second fact shows that this infomation is sufficient to determine what happens when we add a Haar random row vector.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
In this paper, contrary to \cite{arxiv}, the generator of the Markov chain is not described explicitly. Rather, the Markov property is deduced from invariance properties of the Haar measure, as we briefly elaborate below.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
For $u \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\mathcal{C}_u$ is the set of equivalence classes of matrices such that $ \#\text{cols } - \#\text{rows } = u$
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
$\mathcal{C}_u$ has a distinguished element, i.e. the equivalence class of
\[
\begin{mat}{c}
1
\end{mat}
\text{ or }
\begin{mat}{c}
1 \\
\mathbf{0}
\end{mat}
\text{ or }
\begin{mat}{cc}
1 & \mathbf{0}
\end{mat}
\]
We will denote this equivalence class as $O_{u}(R)$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:basechange:k}
A matrix $M$ over $R$ belongs to the equivalence class $O_{u}(R)$ if and only if $M \mod \mathfrak{m}$ belongs to $O_{u}(k)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
A square matrix over $R$ is invertible if and only if its reduction $\mod \mathfrak{m}$ is invertible. \autoref{lem:basechange:k} can be deduced from this fact using row and column operations.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:cokernel}
The map
\[
C_u \xrightarrow{\text{coker}} R-\mathbf{mod}
\]
is well-defined and injective
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
It follows from the definition of the equivalence relation that the map is well-defined. The injectivity follows from the uniqueness of minimal free resolutions of modules over local rings, \cite[Theorem 20.2]{Eisenbud}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
$\text{coker}(O_u(R)) \cong R^{|u|}$ if $u<0$ and $\text{coker}(O_u(R))$ is trivial if $u\geq 0$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This follows from the definition of $O_u(R)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A random operator from $X$ to $Y$ is a linear operator from measures
on $X$ to measures on $Y$, that sends probability measure to
probability measures.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The pro-finite ring $R$ is equipped with a canonical measure,
alternatively called the uniform measure, or the additive Haar measure.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
We say an $R$-valued random variable is Haar random if it is
distributed according to the Haar measure on $R$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:deltar}
(\ref{eqn:deltar}) defines a random operator from $\mathcal{C}_u$ to $\mathcal{C}_u$, for all $u$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We will prove \autoref{thm:deltar} by proving \autoref{lem:deltar} and \autoref{lem:ginvariance}. Together, these will imply \autoref{thm:deltar}.
We will write
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:tilde}
M_1 \sim M_2
\end{equation}
  to denote that $M_1$ and $M_2$ are in the same class in $\mathcal{C}_u$. If
$M_1$ and $M_2$ are random matrices, (\ref{eqn:tilde}) will mean that the two matrices induce the same distribution on $\mathcal{C}_u$. 

\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:deltar}
\[
\begin{mat}{ccc|ccc|c}
&& & && &*
\\
&M& & &\mathbf{0}& &\vdots
\\
&& & &&  &*
\\\hline
&& & &&  &*
\\
&\mathbf{0}& & &\mathbf{I}&  &\vdots
\\
&& & &&  &*
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&* & * &\hdots& * &*
\end{mat}
\sim
\begin{mat}{ccc|ccc|c}
&& & && &*
\\
&M& & &\mathbf{0}& &\vdots
\\
&& & &&  &*
\\\hline
&& & &&  &
\\
&\mathbf{0}& & &\mathbf{I}&  &\mathbf{0}
\\
&& & &&  &
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&* & &  \mathbf{0}&  &*
\end{mat} \sim 
\]
\[
\sim 
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&& &*
\\
&M& &\vdots
\\
&&  &*
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&* & *
\end{mat}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
It suffices to prove
\[
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&&*
\\
&\mathbf{I}&&\vdots
\\
&&&*
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*&*
\end{mat}
\sim
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&&0
\\
&\mathbf{I}&&\vdots
\\
&&&0
\\ \hline
0&\hdots&0&*
\end{mat}
\]

Observe that
\[
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&&
\\
&\mathbf{I}&&\mathbf{v}
\\
&& &
\\ \hline
&\mathbf{w}^{T}&&c
\end{mat}
\
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&&
\\
&\mathbf{I}&&\mathbf{0}
\\
&& &
\\ \hline
&\mathbf{0}&&c - \mathbf{w}^{T} \mathbf{v}
\end{mat}
\]
Now suppose that $c$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are independent
and Haar random. In particular $c$ is Haar random and independent of
$\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{v}$.
\begin{claim}
The sum of two independent random variables is Haar random if one of them is Haar random.
\end{claim}
The claim is a consequence of the fact the Haar distribution is
invariant by translations. It follows that $c - \mathbf{w}^{T}
\mathbf{v}$ is Haar random. This proves \autoref{lem:deltar}.
\end{proof}



\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:ginvariance}
\[
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& *
\\
&g^T M g'&&\vdots
\\
&& &  *
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*&*
\end{mat}
\sim
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& *
\\
&M &&\vdots
\\
&& &  *
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*&*
\end{mat}
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
It suffices to show:
\[
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& *
\\
&g^T M g'&&\vdots
\\
&& &  *
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*&*
\end{mat}=
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& 0
\\
&g&&\vdots
\\
&& &  0
\\ \hline
0&\hdots&0&1
\end{mat}^T
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& *
\\
&M &&\vdots
\\
&& &  *
\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*&*
\end{mat}
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& 0
\\
&g'&&\vdots
\\
&& &  0
\\ \hline
0&\hdots&0&1
\end{mat}
\]
But this follows from the $GL_n(R)$-invariance of the Haar measure on $R^n$, for any $n$. This proves \autoref{lem:deltar} and \autoref{thm:deltar}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
We denote by $\Delta_u$ the random operator induced by
(\ref{eqn:deltar}) on $\mathcal{C}_u$.
\[
M \rightarrow
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& *\\
&M&& \vdots\\
&&& *\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*& *
\end{mat}
\]
\end{definition}
<!-- end head-1 -->

<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
We denote by $\Delta_u$ the random operator induced by
(\ref{eqn:deltar}) on $\mathcal{C}_u$.
\[
M \rightarrow
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&& *\\
&M&& \vdots\\
&&& *\\ \hline
*&\hdots&*& *
\end{mat}
\]
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Recall that $Haar$ be an infinite matrix, whose entries are indexed by
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, with Haar random variables. Recall also that
$Haar_{n,n+u}$ denotes the top-left $n  \times n+u$ minor.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:one}
The random process $\text{coker}\Big(Haar_{n,n+u}\Big)$ is a Markov chain, generated
by the operator $\Delta_u$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:recur}
The Markov chain $\mathbf{c}(Haar_{n,n+u})$ is positive recurrent. Equivalently, the Markov chain \[ \text{coker}(Haar_{n,n+u}) \] is positive recurrent.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:recur}
$O_u(k)$ is a positive recurrent state for the Markov chain
\[
\mathbf{c} (Haar_{n,n+u}(k))
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We prove \autoref{lem:recur} using two standard computations over finite fields:



\begin{itemize}
\item If $u \geq 0$
\[ 
\text{I\kern-0.15em P}(Haar_{n,n+u}(k) \in O_u(k)) =
\]
\[
\text{I\kern-0.15em P}(
corank(Haar_{n,n+u}( k)) = 0
)
=
\prod_{i=u+1}^{n+u} \left(1 - \frac{1}{|k|^i}\right)
\]
\item If $u<0$
\[
\text{I\kern-0.15em P}(Haar_{n,n+u}(k) \in O_u(k)) =
\]
\[
\text{I\kern-0.15em P}(
corank(Haar_{n,n+u}(k)) = |u|
)
=
\prod_{i=|u|+1}^{n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{|k|^i}\right)
\]
\end{itemize}




Hence,
\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \text{I\kern-0.15em P}(Haar_{n,n+u}(k) \in O_u(k))
=
\prod_{i=|u|+1}^\infty \left(1 - \frac{1}{|k|^i}\right)
\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
The operator $\Delta_u$ has a unique stationary measure and the distribution of $c_u \Big( Haar_{n,n+u}(R) \Big)$ converges to this stationary measure.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
From the work of Sawin and Wood, \cite[Lemma 6.6, Lemma 6.7]{SawinWood}, it is possible to give explicit expressions for the measures $\mu_u(R)$, as a measure on modules, when $u \geq 0$. The general expression is given in \cite[Lemma 6.7]{SawinWood}. For the statement that their measure and our measure are the same, see the last line of the penultimate paragraph of \cite[page 48]{SawinWood}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
The two operators in (\ref{eqn:defd}) descend to random operators:
 \[
 d_{u-1,u}: \mathcal{C}_u \rightarrow \mathcal{C}_{u-1}
 \text{ and }
 d_{u+1,u,}: \mathcal{C}_u \rightarrow \mathcal{C}_{u+1},
 \]
 respectively.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The proof is analogous to the proof of \autoref{thm:deltar} above.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
We can similarly define:
 \begin{equation}
 \label{eqn:defdrs}
 d_{r,u}: \, \mathcal{C}_u \rightarrow \mathcal{C}_r
 \end{equation}
 for any $u$ and $r$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. If $u>r$, then (\ref{eqn:defdrs}) is
 defined by adding $|u-r|$ random rows. If $u<r$, (\ref{eqn:defdrs})
 is defined by adding $|u-r|$ random columns. If $u=r$,
 (\ref{eqn:defdrs}) is the identity operator.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:randomoperators}
The operators $d_{r,u}$ satisfy the following identites:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(A)] $d_{r,u} d_{u,s} = d_{r,s}$ whenever $r<u<s$ or $ r >u > s$
\item[(B)] $d_{u,r} d_{r,u} = \Delta_u^{|u-r|}$; in particular $d_{u,u+1}d_{u+1,u}=d_{u,u-1}d_{u-1,u}$
\item[(C)] $d_{r,u}$ is the adjoint of $d_{u,r}$, with respect to the measures $\mu_u$ and $\mu_r$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The first two properties follow immediately from the definitions. The last property is a consequence of \autoref{thm:rev} below.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:rev}
 The operator (\ref{eqn:drs}) defines a \textit{reversible} Markov chain on
 $\mathcal{C}_u \cup \mathcal{C}_r$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:two}
The operator $\Delta_u$ defines a \textit{reversible} Markov chain on
 $\mathcal{C}_u$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:rev}
 Suppose that $\mathcal{M}$ is a $n \times n+u$ random matrix, whose
 distribution is invariant under the action of $GL_{n} \times
 GL_{n+u}$. Then the total variation distance between the distributions of:



\[
\mathbf{c} 
\begin{mat}{ccc|ccc}
&&&*&\hdots&*\\
&&&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
&\mathcal{M}&&*&\hdots&*\\ \cline{4-6}
&&&*&\hdots&*\\
&&&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
&&&*&\hdots&*
\end{mat}
 \hspace{0.25in}
\text{ and }  \hspace{0.25in}
\mathbf{c} 
\begin{mat}{ccc|ccc}
&&&&&\\
&&&&\mathbf{0}&\\
&\mathcal{M}&&&&\\ \cline{4-6}
&&&&&\\
&&&&\mathbf{I}_{r-u}&\\
&&&&&
\end{mat}
 
\]




 is bounded by $o(n)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{G}_{n+u}(R)$ denote a multiplicatively Haar random element of $GL_{n+u}(R)$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Note that the column vectors the matrix on the left of (\ref{eqn:GHaar}) are the first $r-u$ column vectors of $\mathcal{G}$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:technical}
 The distribution of the last $r-u$ vectors of $\mathcal{G}_{n+u}(R)$ is
 the restriction of the additive Haar measure to the set of all $(r-u)$-tuples of vectors that have full $k$-rank.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For the proof of \autoref{lem:technical}, we will use the following standard fact, that we give without proof.
 \begin{sublemma}
 \label{sublem:orbit}
 Let $N$ be any natural number. Every $(r-u)$-tuple of vectors in $R^N$ that are $k$-independent, can be completed to an $N$-tuple of $k$-independent vectors.
\end{sublemma}



 
\paragraph{Proof of \autoref{lem:technical} when $R$ is finite:} Suppose $R$ is finite. Then $GL_{n+u}(R)$ is finite. Applying a uniformly random element of $GL_{n+u}(R)$ to
 \begin{equation}
 \label{eqn:iomatrix}
 \begin{mat}{ccc}
&&\\
&\mathbf{0}&\\
&&\\ \hline
&&\\
&\mathbf{I}_{r-u}& \\
&&\\
\end{mat} 
\end{equation}
 produces a uniformly random element in the orbit of $GL_{n+u}(R)$ acting on (\ref{eqn:iomatrix}). By \autoref{sublem:orbit}, the orbit of $GL_{n+u}(R)$ acting on (\ref{eqn:iomatrix}) consists of all $(r-u)$-tuples of $k$-independent vectors in $R^N$. Hence, we have proven \autoref{lem:technical} for finite $R$
 
\paragraph{Proof of \autoref{lem:technical} when $R$ is infinite:} Now suppose that $R$ is not finite. Then, by the preceding argument, we know that \autoref{lem:technical} holds modulo any power of the maximal ideal of $R$. Because $R$ is profinite, it also holds that \autoref{lem:technical} is true for $R$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- sublemma-1: body_md -->
\label{sublem:orbit}
 Let $N$ be any natural number. Every $(r-u)$-tuple of vectors in $R^N$ that are $k$-independent, can be completed to an $N$-tuple of $k$-independent vectors.
<!-- end sublemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:ffestimate}
The following expression gives the probability that the rank of an $(r-u) \times (n+u) $ Haar random matrix over $k$ is less than $(r-u)$.
\[
1-\prod_{i=1}^{r-u} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{|k|^{n+u-i+1}} \right) = o(n)
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
This is a standard calculation over finite fields.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
We say a matrix over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is singular if there is a non-trivial
relation between the column vectors of $M$, and a non-trivial relation
between the row vectors of $M$. If a matrix is singular, then every
matrix in its equivalence class in $\mathcal{C}_u$ is also singular.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:rel}
We have the following relations, when $R=\mathbb{Z}_p$:
\begin{itemize}
\item The restriction of $d_{-1,0}$ to non-singular equivalence classes
coincides with the operator $d^{*}$, defined in \cite{arxiv}.
\item The restriction of $d_{0,-1}$ to non-singular equivalence classes
coincides with the operator $d$, defined in \cite{arxiv}.
\item Hence, the operator $\Delta_0 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=\joinrel=} d_{0,-1} d_{-1,0}$, defined
above, coincides with the operator $d d^{*}$, when restricted to
non-singular equivalence classes. (In \cite{arxiv}, the operator $d
d^{*}$ is also denoted by the symbol " $\Delta_0$".)
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The restriction to non-singular equivalences classes is not a serious
restriction for the study of Haar random matrices over $\mathbb{Z}_p$, as in
this case, the singular matrices are contained in a set of measure $0$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
To prove \autoref{thm:rel}, it suffices to show that 
\[
d^{*} \Big( \text{coker}(M) \Big) =
\text{coker}
\begin{mat}{ccc}
&& \\
&M& \\
&& \\ \hline
*&\hdots&*
\end{mat}
\]
for all non-singular $n \times n $ matrices $M$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and 
\[
d \Big( \text{coker}(M) \Big)
=
\text{coker} 
\begin{mat}{ccc|c}
&&&*\\
&M&&\vdots\\
&&&*\\
\end{mat}
\]
for all non-singular $(n +1) \times n$ matrices $M$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
But this is shown in \cite[Theorem 1.1]{arxiv}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
Any ring homomorphism $R \rightarrow R/I$ induces maps:
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:modImap}
red_I: \, C_u (R) \rightarrow C_u (R/I)
\end{equation}
We will call this the \textit{reduction} map. The push-forward of reduction induces an operator from measures on $C_u (R)$ to measures on $C_u (R/I)$. Moreover, we can define
the adjoint of reduction, with respect to the measures $\mu_u(R)$ and
$\mu_u(R/I)$. The adjoint of reduction will be a random operator:
\[
ind_I: \, C_u(R/I) \rightarrow C_u(R)
\] 
We will call this the \textit{induction} operator. We will define a more explicit operator in the following lemma; we will then show that this explicit operator coincides with the induction operator.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:inductionop}
The following is a well-defined random operator from $C_u(R/I)$ to $C_u(R)$.
Given a matrix $M$ over $R/I$, replace every entry of $M$ by an independent Haar random element of its $I$-coset in $R$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:adj}
On matrices equipped with the Haar measure, this operator is the adjoint of reduction modulo $I$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By arguments similar to those in the proof of \autoref{thm:deltar}, we can
verify that this induces a random operator from $C_u(R/I)$ to
$C_u(R)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:opcommutativity}
The operator $red_I$, and the operator defined in \autoref{lem:inductionop} commute with the operators $d_{u,r}$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The commutativity can be verified on the level of matrices.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
The operator defined in \autoref{lem:inductionop} is the same as the operator $ind_I$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Denote the operator defined in  \autoref{lem:inductionop} as $\gamma_I$. First of all, it easy to see that $O_u(R)=\gamma_I O_u(R/I)$ and $O_u(R/I)=red_I O_u(R)$. By \autoref{thm:opcommutativity}, $\Delta_u^N O_u(R)=\gamma_I \Delta_u^N O_u(R/I)$ and $\Delta_u^N O_u(R/I)=red_I \Delta_u^N O_u(R)$.\footnote{The preceding two identities are also a restatement of \autoref{rem:adj}.} Now taking the limit $N\rightarrow \infty$ gives:  $\mu_u(R)=\gamma_I \mu_u(R/I)$ and $\mu_u(R/I)=red_I \mu_u(R)$. Hence, $\gamma_I$ is the adjoint of reduction with respect to the measures $\mu_u(R)$ and $\mu_u(R/I)$
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
(Of \autoref{thm:opcommutativity})
The image of $ind_{I}$ is a subspace of the space of signed measures on 
$C_{ \, \boldsymbol{\cdot} \, }(R)$
that is invariant under the action of the operators 
$d_{ \, \boldsymbol{\cdot} \, , \, \boldsymbol{\cdot} \, }$;
the kernel of $red_{I}$ is also a subspace of the space of signed measures on $C_{ \, \boldsymbol{\cdot} \, } (R)$
that is invariant under the action of the operators 
$d_{ \, \boldsymbol{\cdot} \, , \, \boldsymbol{\cdot} \, }$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
